Treatment of bronchiolitis: state of the art
Liviana Da Dalt a,b , Silvia Bressan a , Francesco Martinolli a , Giorgio Perilongo a , Eugenio Baraldi a, *
a Women's and Child's Health Department, Unit of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine and Allergy, Unit of Pediatric Emergency Department, University of Padova, Italy b
Pediatric Unit, Treviso Hospital, Italy
a r t i c l e i n f o
Keywords: Bronchiolitis Lower respiratory tract infection Bronchodilators Corticosteroids High flow nasal cannulae Hypertonic saline
1. Introduction

Bronchiolitis is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in the first year of life, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the pathogen most often responsible for it (in 60-85% of cases). Other agents, especially human rhinovirus, have been associated with bronchiolitis. Most children with bronchiolitis have mild disease and are managed at home with support from primary care providers alone. Children with more severe symptoms nonetheless account for the majority of hospital admissions in the first 12 months of life and some will need ventilatory support [1]. RSV infection carries significant morbidity and mortality rates, especially in prematurely born infants ( < 35 weeks of gestational age) and infants with major health issues, such as chronic lung disease (i.e. bronchopulmonary dysplasia or cystic fibrosis), or hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease. Cases of severe illness occur mostly in babies between 2 and 3 months of age, corresponding to the natural postnatal nadir of protective maternal immunoglobulins received through the placenta during the last trimester of pregnancy. s u m m a r y

Bronchiolitis is a leading cause of acute illness and hospitalization for infants and young children worldwide. It is usually a mild disease, but the few children developing severe symptoms need to be hospitalized and some will need ventilatory support. To date, the mainstay of therapy has been supportive care, i.e. assisted feeding and hydration, minimal handling, nasal suctioning and oxygen therapy. In recent years the delivery of oxygen has been improved by using a highflow nasal cannula. At the same time, the discovery of nebulized hypertonic saline enables better airway cleaning with a benefit for respiratory function. The possible role of any pharmacological approach is still debated: many pharmacological therapies tried in the past, ranging from bronchodilators to corticosteroids, were found to offer no benefit in this disease. More recently, nebulized adrenaline demonstrated a short-term benefit. Prophylaxis and prevention, especially in children at high risk of severe infection, such as prematurely born infants and children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, have a fundamental role in dealing with this disease. In this review, we focus on current recommendations for the management and prevention of bronchiolitis, paying particular attention to the latest literature in search of answers to the questions that remain open.

RSV infections are common even in the same season. The chances of severe symptoms may be further increased by the development of chronic lung disease or other conditions limiting pulmonary functional reserves. Additional risk factors for severe disease include: male gender; crowding; lack of breastfeeding; low socio-economic status; exposure to indoor smoke pollution; daycare attendance; siblings in the family; birth during certain periods of the year; and any type of immunodeficiency [2,3].

The type and frequency of diagnostic tests prescribed for bronchiolitis, such as pulse oximetry, virus detection and radiography, vary considerably from one clinician to another [4], and many controversies still exist as to the best therapeutic approach in relation to the severity of the disease.

The present review covers the most recent evidencebased developments on the management and prevention of bronchiolitis, focusing particularly on the treatment options available outside the intensive care setting (Table 1).
2. Supportive therapy
2.1. Oxygen therapy and high-flow nasal cannula oxygen administration
Despite the growing body of literature investigating treatment options, oxygen supplementation remains the mainstay of therapy for bronchiolitis [4].

Oxygen therapy administered via a heated humidified highflow nasal cannula (HFNC) has recently been introduced in clinical practice and is gaining widespread popularity -even outside the intensive care setting -because it has proved to be a well-tolerated, non-invasive form of respiratory support [16-18]. HFNC provides a humidified and heated blend of air and oxygen at a flow rate of 1-8L/min, compared to the maximum flow of 2L/min recommended with traditional oxygen therapy. The HFNC is thought to improve ventilatory status by preventing mucus dryness and improving mucousciliary clearance and delivering a continuous positive airway pressure, which helps to keep the alveoli patent, improves the ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and prevents microatelectasis (commonly occurring as a pathophysiological consequence of terminal airway inflammation and obstruction) [19-21].

The continuous positive airway pressure provided by the HFNC has shown to increase with the flow rate administered [22], but the pressure applied to the pharynx by the circuit cannot be measured and regulated as it can with nasal-CPAP. The latter is often poorly tolerated, however, and is impractical outside the intensive care setting [23,24].

The first studies on the effect of the HFNC in children with bronchiolitis were carried out at intensive care units [16,17]. Their retrospective data showed a reduction in the intubation rate and an improvement in the respiratory distress associated with the introduction of HFNC.

A more recent randomized controlled pilot study (HFNC vs head box oxygen) on 19 patients found a higher SpO 2 in patients receiving HFNC oxygen (SpO 2 100% vs 96%, p = 0.04) [18]. While the effect on respiratory distress was not assessed, there was no difference in length of hospitalization or time to return to feeding.

A pilot study conducted by our group showed that the HFNC is a feasible oxygen delivery method in infants with moderatesevere bronchiolitis hospitalized in a pediatric ward setting, and it is associated with improvement in respiratory rate and endtidal carbon dioxide [25].

Although the HFNC seems a promising form of respiratory support for use even outside the intensive care setting, randomized controlled studies are needed to investigate its safety and effectiveness in reducing hospital stays and the need for transfer to the intensive care unit, as well as its long-term benefits and economic impact on the healthcare system.

In addition, a recent report of serious air leak syndrome complicating HFNC therapy in an infant with bronchiolitis [26] underscores the need for extreme caution in using HFNC for the off-label indication of providing positive distending pressure in children, especially at flows higher than the patient's minute ventilation.

Two studies are currently underway to further evaluate the real impact of the HFNC on important outcomes, such as hospital stay and admission to the ICU, and its ability to improve clinical scores. (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/results?term= bronchiolitis+and+%22high+flow+oxygen%22&Search=Search).
2.2. Nasal suctioning

Published guidelines recommend superficial suctioning to clear the nostrils of secretions to improve airway patency, particularly in younger infants [5,6,27]. This should be done before assessing SpO2 and can ease oral intake if it is performed before the child feeds. There is no evidence to support the use of deep pharyngeal suctioning in children with bronchiolitis.
2.3. Feeding and hydration

Fluid administration is an important intervention in children with bronchiolitis, whose ability to feed properly is impaired by their moderate-severe respiratory distress, bouts of coughing and upper respiratory secretions. For mild cases, feeding more frequently in smaller amounts is better tolerated and breastfeeding should not be suspended. For moderate and severe cases, there is a marked variability in clinical practice, with some centers opting for intravenous fluid administration and others preferring the nasogastric route [28]. Nasogastric feeding has proved a safe alternative to intravenous fluid administration in children with bronchiolitis. The recent, and largest to date, randomized controlled trial on bronchiolitis carried out in Australia and New Zealand found no differences in terms of length of stay, admission to ICUs, need for ventilatory support or adverse events between the two types of intervention [29]. Inserting the nasogastric tube should take fewer attempts, however, and have a higher success rate than implementing intravenous hydration.

2.4. Chest physiotherapy and mist-steam
While there is insufficient evidence to show any benefit of mist-steam in bronchiolitis [9], chest physiotherapy has proved ineffective [8].
2.5. Hypertonic saline

In recent years, a growing body of literature has supported the use of nebulized hypertonic saline (HS). The mechanisms of its action are well described in the paper by Mandelberg and Amirav [30], and include a reduction in airway edema, a greater mucus clearance and less viscous secretions. Studies investigating the usefulness of 3% HS have been conducted in the past 10 years and have included both outpatients and inpatients. Recent reviews [7,31,32] have highlighted a divergence between the results of studies conducted on already hospitalized patients (for whom HS was found to reduce the hospital stay) and studies that included emergency department patients (using HS was not effective in reducing the hospital admission rate, although it coincided with a transient improvement in clinical severity score). These results support the hypothesis that HS is useful when delivered repeatedly and assessed in terms of longer-term outcomes, but less so as a single dose and with short-term outcome.

Despite the lack of strong evidence to recommend the routine use of HS for the treatment of bronchiolitis, its high safety profile, low cost and non-invasive administration make it a reasonable option for treating children with bronchiolitis. A recent article by Ralston and colleagues [33] showed that it is safe even when administered alone without salbutamol, refuting previous concerns that administering HS could trigger bronchospasm and should be given together with bronchodilators. Only one study so far has evaluated the usefulness of 5% HS, finding a good safety profile and a greater effectiveness than with normal saline, but no difference compared with 3% HS [32,34].

Several randomized controlled trials are currently underway on the effectiveness of HS in bronchiolitis and will soon provide better evidence to support strong recommendations on its use (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/results?term=hypertonic+ saline+AND+bronchiolitis&pg=2).
3. Pharmacological therapy
3.1. Beta-agonists

The results of two recent systematic reviews [10,11] showed that nebulized bronchodilators are ineffective in the treatment of bronchiolitis, supporting the recommendations of previous guidelines [5,6,27]. Bronchodilators are unable to improve oxygen saturation, the hospital admission rate, the length of hospital stays, or the time to recovery at home.
The mild improvement in clinical scores associated with the use of bronchodilators has to be balanced against the risk of their side effects and their cost.
3.2. Adrenaline

According to the most recent available evidence, nebulized adrenaline seems to be the only pharmacological therapy showing some effectiveness in the treatment of bronchiolitis. Administering adrenaline has revealed positive effects on shortterm measures, improving the clinical score and reducing admission rates in the first 24 hours of care. No benefits have been observed for inpatients, however [11,12,35]. Given the shortage of studies and its potential adverse effects, adrenaline is not recommended in the home setting [5].
3.3. Steroids

Both systemic and inhaled steroids have been amply investigated as a treatment for bronchiolitis. The results of these studies have recently been summarized in high-quality systematic reviews and meta-analyses [11,13,14]. No clinically relevant effects of either systemic or inhaled steroids were found in terms of admission rates or length of hospitalization. In addition, inhaled steroids given during the acute phase of bronchiolitis have had no effect in preventing post-bronchiolitis wheezing [14].
3.4. Combinations of adrenaline and steroids

The Canadian multicenter randomized double-blind, placebocontrolled trial recently published by Plint and colleagues [36] was the first to find a positive effect of a combined therapy with nebulized adrenaline and oral dexamethasone. However, the very high doses of dexamethasone (1mg/kg followed by 0.6 mg/kg for the next 5 days) and the prolonged treatment in this young age group raise concern as regards the possible long-term effects on the child's neurocognitive development, given the lack of data on the combination's long-term safety. In addition, this study was not initially planned to specifically investigate the effects of the combination of adrenaline and dexamethasone, so it was not adequately powered for this analysis and the results failed to reach statistical significance when the adjusted analysis was performed. Even the biological plausibility of the efficacy of such a combined therapy remains to be clarified [35].
3.5. Antibiotics

The use of antibiotics in children with bronchiolitis has long been discussed. The guidelines recommend antibiotics only when a bacterial co-infection is identified or highly likely [5,6,27]. A recent Cochrane review [37] found only minimal evidence to support the use of antibiotics in bronchiolitis, and called for further research to identify subgroups of patients (i.e. patients with chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant heart disease, hospitalized in intensive care) who might benefit most from the use of antibiotics.

It has also been suggested that macrolides may be useful in treating bronchiolitis because of their anti-inflammatory immunomodulatory effect. Previous studies generated conflicting results [38,39], however, and the most recent randomized controlled trial found no benefit of macrolides in children with bronchiolitis, recommending against their use, given that overuse increases overall antibiotic resistance [40].
3.6. Antiviral agents

bronchiolitis. Its use is not routinely recommended by current guidelines [5,6,27]. According to a recent Cochrane review [41] there are insufficient data to provide reliable estimates on its effects in bronchiolitis. Given uncertainty about its effectiveness and the lack of data on its safety, this treatment option might be considered only for children with severe disease, or underlying conditions that predispose them to more severe presentation, such as immunodeficiencies, chronic lung disease or haemodynamically significant heart diseases [5].
3.7. Other pharmacological options

Although high leukotriene concentrations have been found in the respiratory secretions of children with bronchiolitis, suggesting a pathogenic role of these mediators in bronchiolitis [42], conflicting results have been reported on the effectiveness of antileukotriene medication such as montelukast, and no systematic reviews on the topic have been published so far [43,44]. Even the possible role of montelukast in preventing recurrent respiratory symptoms after bronchiolitis remains to be clarified [45-48].

Conflicting results have also emerged on the use of nebulized DNase - believed to improve airway clearance of secretions thanks to its mucolytic properties [49-51] - and the latest Cochrane review does not support its use in children with bronchiolitis [15].
Only one study has investigated the use of nebulized furosemide, which was found ineffective [52].

As for RSV bronchiolitis-associated apneas, only case series have shown a benefit of methylxanthines, such as caffeine and theophylline, as a consequence of their central respiratory stimulant effect [53,54], while most severe cases may need ventilatory support. However, even though epidemiological data on the prevalence of this condition are lacking [55], any evidence of the effectiveness of medical treatment will have a significant impact on the treatment of young infants, who more often present with RSV-related apneas.
4. Future therapeutic perspectives

It has recently been shown in both animal models and adult humans infected with RSV, that antiviral therapy based on RNA interference may be an effective treatment for bronchiolitis [56]. RNA interference is a natural mechanism regulating protein expression that is mediated by small interfering RNAs. Intranasal administration of small interfering RNA targeting specific RSV gene expression may change the approach to the treatment of bronchiolitis in the future [57].
5. Prevention/prophylaxis
The absence of an effective treatment for bronchiolitis makes prevention the best choice to reduce the burden of the disease and its impact on social health [3].

In recent years, immunoprophylaxis with palivizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody capable of neutralizing RSV, has proved effective in reducing hospitalization rates relating to RSV infections [58-60]. This prophylaxis cannot be offered to the whole population of children under 24 months of age because of its high cost. The current recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) for the management of bronchiolitis identify specific groups of children found to benefit from prophylaxis with palivizumab (Table 2) and the minimal number of doses needed to guarantee an effective protection [5,61].

Other groups of high-risk patients who could benefit from palivizumab prophylaxis, i.e. children with cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiencies, have recently been evaluated in different studies and palivizumab has proved safe and effective in these children as well [62,63].

It is important not to forget that, although RSV accounts for the majority of cases, it is not the only virus implicated in bronchiolitis. General prevention strategies to combat the risk factors, as well as parent and caregiver education, must therefore remain the first line of intervention for clinicians [2]. Frequent handwashing, avoiding exposing children to tobacco smoke [64], and breastfeeding have proved very effective in protecting infants and children against lower respiratory tract infections (and RSVrelated ones in particular) [2,5].

An interesting field in the prevention of bronchiolitis concerns the relationship between respiratory viral infections and vitamin D. A deficiency of vitamin D has been seen to increase the risk of viral respiratory tract infections and RSV-associated bronchiolitis [65]. A recent prospective birth cohort study demonstrated that children who are vitamin D deficient at birth have a six-fold risk of developing RSV bronchiolitis in the first year of life [66]. These preliminary data suggest that action to change the vitamin D status of mothers during pregnancy and/or vitamin D supplementation of infants could reduce the risk of RSV-associated bronchiolitis.
6. Conclusion

In summary, available evidence shows that administering oxygen and clearing the upper airways of secretions is still the mainstay of treatment for bronchiolitis. HFNC oxygen delivery seems a promising non-invasive mode of respiratory support, but further studies are needed to better define its role in the treatment of children with bronchiolitis outside the intensive care setting. Nasogastric feeding has proved safe and just as effective as intravenous fluid administration. Hypertonic saline seems to be effective in reducing the hospital stay for inpatients, while mist-steam and chest physiotherapy appear to have no role in treating bronchiolitis.

Of the pharmacological options, nebulized adrenaline is the only medication found to be effective in reducing admission rates in the first 24 hours after assessment at the emergency department, but there is still no evidence of its usefulness for inpatients. The available data on the effectiveness of combining adrenaline with high doses of dexamethasone cannot support the routine use of this treatment option and only further studies could clarify its real efficacy and long-term effects.
The intranasal administration of antiviral therapy based on RNA interference may change the therapeutic approach to bronchiolitis in the future.
Immunoprophylaxis with palivizumab remains the recommended prevention therapy for children at high risk of severe bronchiolitis.
Vitamin D may help to prevent respiratory tract infections, but further studies are needed to better clarify its role in bronchiolitis prophylaxis.
